A.explanation: Mass of $1.0\text{ kg}$ is correct, but weight must increase where $g$ is larger, not decrease to $0.1\text{ N}$.

B.explanation: Mass stays $1.0\text{ kg}$ and weight becomes $10$ times larger, $10\text{ N}$, because $g$ on Q is $10$ times $g$ on P.

C.explanation: Weight of $10\text{ N}$ is correct, but mass does not change with planet and remains $1.0\text{ kg}$, not $10\text{ kg}$.

D.explanation: Both values are wrong because mass is invariant and weight scales only by the factor $10$ in $g$, giving $1.0\text{ kg}$ and $10\text{ N}$.

hints: Notice the question moves the same object from planet P to planet Q, so ask yourself which quantity, mass in $\text{kg}$ or weight in $\text{N}$, depends on location.
Recall $W = m g$ on each planet, and use the $1.0\text{ kg}$ and $1.0\text{ N}$ on P to find $g$ on P.
Since $g$ on P is one-tenth of $g$ on Q, $g$ on Q is ten times larger, so multiply the same mass by the larger $g$ to get the new weight.
walkthrough: On planet P the object has $m = 1.0\text{ kg}$ and $W = 1.0\text{ N}$. Mass measures amount of matter, so for the same object it does not change when the planet changes.
Weight is the gravitational force, $W = m g$, where $g$ is the acceleration of free fall on that planet.
Find $g$ on P: $g_P = W_P / m = 1.0\text{ N} / 1.0\text{ kg} = 1.0\text{ N kg}^{-1}$.
The question states $g_P$ is one-tenth of $g_Q$, so $g_Q = 10 \times g_P = 10 \times 1.0\text{ N kg}^{-1} = 10\text{ N kg}^{-1}$.
Calculate weight on Q for the same mass: $W_Q = m g_Q = 1.0\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ N kg}^{-1} = 10\text{ N}$.
Mass on Q is $1.0\text{ kg}$ and weight on Q is $10\text{ N}$. This is option B
